title: How the Western Bulldogs engineered a return to AFLW finals
text:
It's a story that's been told countless times. The Western Bulldogs hit rock bottom in 2023, opted to undertake a review into their program, and made wholesale change. Since then, they've made steady improvement, but that hasn't been without some rocky moments along the way.

Now, the Bulldogs are locked into finals for the first time since 2022 and present as a genuine threat in the post-season, rather than simply making up the numbers.

And while their off-field changes have been immense, and an easy starting point when it comes to analysing their improvement, what has happened on field is even more interesting.

Rock bottom

The Bulldogs finished 2023 as wooden spooners, winning one game from 10 rounds of footy just a year after reaching its second ever final. Across that season they gave up control in-game easily, and relied heavily on a small handful of players to carry the load.

This required a personnel change to start the improvement spike. A new head coach, head of footy and list manager were certainly key to the shift, but change on field was also essential.

From the playing list that reached a final in 2022 just 12 players remain, and while the club has largely focused on careful draft selections, it has also engaged in trades to add experience on top of the youth.

Listed in 2022 S7 Added since Elle Bennetts Deanna Berry Ellie Blackburn Alice Edmonds Jess Fitzgerald Elisabeth Georgostathis Isabella Grant Britney Gutknecht Sarah Hartwig Isabelle Pritchard Rylie Wilcox

Heidi Woodley Lauren Ahrens (trade) Brooke Barwick (draft) Mizuki Brothwell (draft) Cleo Buttifant (draft) Mikala Cann (trade) Dom Carruthers (draft) Ellie Gavalas (trade) Maggie Gorham (free agent) Elaine Grigg (draft) Keeley Hardingham (draft) Kaylee Kimber (replacement) Vaomua Laloifi (trade) Emma McDonald (draft) Analea McKee (trade) Charlie O'Connor Moreira (draft) Sarah Poustie (draft) Jasmyn Smith (trade) Lou Stephenson (trade) Amaia Wain (draft)

This list build has happened quietly. There are no boom recruits among the incoming trades, no premiership players or All-Australians in the mix as other clubs have targeted, but they have been specific choices to work toward the game plan.

Mikala Cann has been one of those players. Little more than a role player at Collingwood, albeit a very good one, Cann has been exactly the kind of midfielder/forward required at the Dogs to elevate the team as a whole.

The stat changing Geelong in 2026 When Geelong made the move to bring Mick Stinear to the cattery, it made a bigger difference to their 2026 season than any player movement could.

Outside of this, the club's capacity to improve some down-and-out senior players has also been important.

Mua Laloifi has emerged on the other side of an ACL injury in close to her best career form, offering important intercepting strength behind the ball, and Ellie Gavalas has spent a couple of years in the wilderness but now adds some leadership and ground-level speed in the forward half.

And the draftees have been carefully selected. Although some choices haven't quite come on in the way the club would have hoped — every club has been burned by a speculative pick here or there — others have been the ideal slow burn.

Emma McDonald and Elaine Grigg were arguably the Dogs' biggest-name draftees across this period, but others like Cleo Buttifant and Dom Carruthers have complemented the growth of the list.

The Bulldogs are becoming a team that is clearly greater than simply the sum of its parts. The puzzle as a whole works well together.

Build defence

The traditional route for a club's rebuild is to start with defence, then add attack, and that's exactly the direction the Bulldogs went once Tam Hyett was appointed coach in 2024.

They were coming off a base that was easy to win the ball against, easy to maintain momentum against, and ultimately far too easy to score against.

Taking back control

Avg disposals conceded Avg uncontested possessions conceded Avg disposal efficiency conceded (%) Avg marks conceded 2026 236.4 120.6 61.8 51.2 2025 241.1 124.9 62.0 44.4 2024 241.9 128.5 63.0 50.2 2023 269.4 155.9 66.6 56.2

Finding that defensive mindset isn't simply about establishing a strong backline, rather as the numbers above suggest, it is about making the game scrappy at times to prevent the opposition from clean access at the footy.

No longer are the Bulldogs walkovers around the footy, or easy to maintain possession against around the ground. When a team plays the Bulldogs, they are to expect a battle around the contest and pressure on the outside.

This, then, leant into tightening up on the scoreboard.

Becoming harder to score against

Avg points against Avg I50s conceded Avg marks I50 conceded Avg shots per I50 conceded (%) Avg shots on goal conceded 2026 32.3 32.5 7.7 36.9 12.0 2025 32.1 28.1 4.8 38.6 10.8 2024 41.9 31.5 7.4 43.1 13.6 2023 59.5 37.5 11.3 52.3 19.6

To get here they played some admittedly ugly footy (everyone remembers that 2024 game against the Bombers), but the first step in the plan has been the foundation upon which everything else has been built. And although some of those numbers have swung slightly back up (specifically inside 50s and marks inside 50 conceded), this has been a result of now working to find the balance between defence and attack.

Learn to attack

In Hyett's first year at the helm, the Bulldogs had their worst year in attack since the AFLW began, averaging just 26.5 points per game. Things seemed bleak and the end of the tunnel felt a long way away. But steadily, on top of that tightening defence, they have also found their own confidence to attack.

As with the defensive tightening, the first part is establishing more control through the middle of the ground, then the next layer is engaging those forwards close to goal to actually get scores on the board.

Winning the footy

Avg handballs Avg kick rate (%) Avg uncontested possessions 2026 120.3 55.5 148.4 2025 99.8 59.6 122.8 2024 70.7 64.4 95.2 2023 93.1 61.8 135.3

Getting their hands on the footy has been a key part to winning back control throughout games, but part of that has also been a shift in how they want to use the ball.

Instead of dump kicking the ball long to escape danger or opting for long down-the-line kicks to a contest where they can compete again, the Dogs are now establishing a clear handball game; moving neatly from layers around the contest via hand and looking for the running handball receive option to add speed on the ball.

That outside ball has been a huge growth area as they develop more confidence in their game style, and for the first time since 2022 the club is averaging a positive uncontested possession differential.

Kicking a winning score

Avg points for Avg I50s Avg shots on goal Avg shots per I50 (%) 2026 45.5 32.9 14.8 20.1 2025 40.6 34.3 14.6 16.1 2024 26.5 27.0 9.3 13.5 2023 32.0 27.4 10.8 16.4

A whole new forward line has been built, with Sarah Hartwig becoming the club's all-time leading goalkicker back in round nine, and Emma McDonald posting the most goals of any Dog in 2025, her debut season.

It has been a calm, steady club-wide build that has flown under the radar in the context of the wild swings that occur in the AFLW, but it has been done for the long haul.

And in a fortnight, the Dogs will get a chance to show their wares in finals, and are a good chance of winning their first final since their flag in 2018.

title: Spirit ferries, terminals have millions wiped in major asset write-down
text:
The operator of the Spirit of Tasmania ferries has announced a $723 million accounting loss for the year, but insists the state-owned company's outlook is "very strong".

The bulk of TT-Line's accounting loss in 2025–26 relates to a $646.9 million write-down of assets, including its four ferries and two terminals.

A write-down is when an asset is reassessed as having a lower value to the company than what it was listed on the balance sheet as.

"I'm not seeking to suggest that's not significant," TT-Line chairman Ken Kanofski said.

"But it is non-cash, and it has no impact on our equity ask. It has no impact on our debt position.

"And to that extent, it's really the accounting catching up with all the issues that have been well publicised for some time now."

In May, it was revealed the company's much-maligned ferry replacement program had cost $717 million more than originally expected.

In the same month, the government announced a $506 million equity injection into TT-Line, and later increased the company's borrowing limit by $410 million.

The new write-downs include:

Spirit of Tasmania I and II — from $174.3 million to $87.5 million

— from $174.3 million to $87.5 million Spirit of Tasmania IV and V — from $1.086 billion to $717.9 million

— from $1.086 billion to $717.9 million Devonport terminal — from $416.8 million to $282.8 million

— from $416.8 million to $282.8 million Geelong terminal — from $311 million to $262.1 million

Ken Kanofski (right) says TT-Line's lender TasCorp and state Treasurer Eric Abetz (left) have also approved changes to the debt repayment due dates. (ABC News)

Like new car leaving showroom, chairman says

Spirit I made its final voyage across Bass Strait on Thursday, and Spirit II will do the same on Friday evening.

Bungled ferry replacement project cost $717m more than forecast The Spirit of Tasmania ferry replacement program has cost $717 million more than was forecast in the original business case, a parliamentary inquiry has heard.

Mr Kanofski said several parties were interested in buying either one or both vessels.

He said the significant write-downs for the older ships reflected decreased demand from buyers due to unrest in the Middle East, higher interest rates and the type of fuel the ships use.

For the new ships, which begin servicing Bass Strait at the end of the month, Mr Kanofski likened their write-downs to the reduced value of a new car once it leaves the showroom.

He also downplayed the revaluations of the Devonport and Geelong terminals.

"Of course it's material, but it doesn't change anything," he said.

"So we're not asking for more equity. It doesn't change the way we're going to trade.

" We're not asking for more debt, so it doesn't change the fundamentals of the business. "

Along with the new ferries, Tasmania has invested in the construction of a new ferry terminal in Devonport. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Mr Kanofski said TT-Line had recorded a $1.5 million operating profit last financial year.

Buyer still wanted for Spirit of Tasmania ferries With their final voyage imminent, the future of ferries Spirit I and II is unclear, with no buyer yet and no local berths available to store them.

While acknowledging the company still faced financial challenges, he insisted it was in good shape for the future.

"I think the outlook is very strong," he said.

"I mean, the reality is we've now got very, very good assets.

"They're all brand new, the berths are brand new, the ships are brand new.

"It's not unusual early in the life of large-scale infrastructure for the returns to be less than what you would hope for."

He said the company's lender, TasCorp, and state Treasurer Eric Abetz had also approved changes to the dates its debt repayments were due.

"We've been solvent at all times, and we remain that way," Mr Kanofski said.

title: New York City bans horse-drawn carriages from 2028
text:
The New York City Council has voted to ban horse-drawn carriages from city streets and Central Park, ending a historic tourist attraction and longstanding industry.

Forty of the city's 51 council members supported the bill, which was backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who earlier this month said the horse-drawn carriage industry would come to an end.

Seven voted against it and two abstained.

If the mayor signs it, the ban will go into effect in June of 2028.

The ban comes after decades of debate about the practice and the recent death of an Indian tourist.

The lead-up is meant to help the approximately 150 active carriage drivers find new employment, city council speaker Julie Menin said.

Critics say the animals suffer, pointing to deadly collapses and dangerous escapes, while advocates point to the jobs they create and the heritage they uphold.

The bill included a provision for exploring potential compensation for licence holders, Ms Menin said.

The Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage business owners and drivers, opposes the ban. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

It prevents owners of the nearly 200 horses from selling them for slaughter or for other horse-carriage businesses.

Support for the ban grew after the death this summer of Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old tourist from India.

Mr Mahajan was thrown from a carriage and died on June 17, when the horse ​bolted after the driver stepped away to take a picture of Mahajan's family.

Romanch Mahajan's family react to the council vote to phase out horse-drawn carriages. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

That followed a series of other incidents with the carriages, including the deaths of several horses.

The Central Park Conservancy, which manages the US's most frequented urban park with 42 million annual visits, threw its weight behind the calls for a ban, saying it had become "a matter of public health and safety".

US President Donald Trump, who has both attacked Mamdani and held cordial meetings with him, expressed scepticism about the ban.

Forty of the city's 51 council members supported the bill. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

"When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don't stop cars from entering the Park," Mr Trump wrote.

" So why would they stop the Carriages? It was a Great Tradition. Another piece of History that's gone. It will be missed! "

Mr Trump's business empire is headquartered in Trump Tower, minutes from Central Park.

The day before the vote, the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage business owners and drivers, said that if the bill was enacted, it would seek a temporary restraining order from a court "the minute the ink dries", according to a letter sent to New York City Corporation counsel Steve Banks.

"This may be the first time in City history that a previously licensed profession was banned," the letter signed by principal attorney Arthur Schwartz said.

"The proposed bill deprives the owner of all economically beneficial or productive use of their property."

Reuters/AFP

title: How to transform an underused balcony into a lush, functional living space
text:
For Tilly Bissett and Nick Billings, like many apartment dwellers, their balcony felt like an afterthought: a place for a few pots, a chair or two and not much else.

But with some clever planning they transformed the narrow 11-square-metre space in Richmond, Melbourne, into a thriving outdoor room packed with greenery, edible plants and distinct zones for everyday living.

A beautiful but underused space

The couple's north-facing balcony had plenty of potential, but they weren't sure how to make the most of it.

Wide view of Tilly and Nick’s balcony before the garden makeover, with sparse planting and existing furniture. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

A keen cook and entertainer, Tilly wanted a space where she could grow some produce to use in the kitchen.

Despite trying a few different plants, she had found the balcony a challenging space to garden.

What followed was a rethink of how the space functioned and what could be grown there.

Think bigger with plants

One of the most significant changes was replacing a collection of small hanging herb pots with a few larger feature plants.

These created immediate focal points that helped define the balcony and gave a sense of greenery.

A large Queensland bottle tree sits beside potted plants against a wall. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

A bottle tree (Brachychiton rupestris) in a sunny position became the main feature tree. Not usually grown in pots, bottle trees grow slowly, meaning they are a low-maintenance option for time-poor gardeners.

Another large pot with a lemon myrtle (Backhousia citriodora) provided an attractive edible tree in a more sheltered spot.

Large potted plants fill a balcony corner beside a window, creating a lush green screen and adding privacy to the space. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

To complete the look, a third large pot was planted with a bay laurel (Laurus nobilis) in the hot, sunny spot next to the barbecue.

A balcony garden in the making, with a small plant being potted into a ceramic container alongside other established pots. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

Weight is an important consideration when gardening on a balcony. Tilly chose lightweight pots and mixed perlite through a premium potting mix to reduce the overall load on the structure, while still giving plants the room they need to thrive.

Growing food in a small space

A dedicated food-growing area was included at one end of the balcony.

Rather than installing permanent structures, modular wicking beds were built from second-hand containers sourced through Facebook Marketplace.

The stacked containers raise the growing beds off the ground and allow veggies to receive sunlight for much of the day, while putting them at a height that makes harvesting easy.

Wicking beds featuring betel leaf, leafy greens and strawberries. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

The wicking design also means the beds only need watering once a week in winter and a couple of times a week in summer.

Filled with herbs, leafy greens and other edible crops, the new kitchen garden gives Tilly a ready supply of ingredients just steps from the kitchen.

Strawberries emerging among the productive planting in the wicking bed. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

Layering greenery from floor to ceiling

Another key to the transformation was making use of vertical space.

Layering greenery at different heights created a much richer and more immersive feeling than relying on pots at ground level alone.

The balcony now features plants across multiple levels, including wall planters filled with epiphytes, a striking elkhorn fern (Platycerium bifurcatum) mounted on a backing board attached to the wall and climbing edibles growing up a wire trellis.

Elkhorn fern is a great choice for balcony gardens, adding height and vertical interest without taking up much floor space. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

Small, medium and large pots throughout the space added further layers of foliage. Tilly and Nick repotted their monsteras and added philodendrons, rubber tree (Ficus elastica) and bird's nest fern (Asplenium cv.) to get a mix of colours and textures.

The result is a balcony that feels lush but not overcrowded.

A wide view of the completed balcony garden, showing how the space has been transformed into a lush and productive outdoor room for relaxing, growing and entertaining. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

"I wouldn't have thought that so many plants could fit on the balcony, to be honest," Tilly says, "[but] it feels like there's still a lot of space here."

Using zoning in small spaces

One useful lesson from the project is that zoning isn't just for large backyards. Despite the balcony's small size, it now contains three distinct areas: a barbecue and dining zone, a productive food garden and a cosy reading nook.

A practical balcony entertaining area combining seating, potted plants and a barbecue, with a timber storage cupboard beneath the barbecue making clever use of the limited space. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

The different spaces aren't heavily separated, but each serves a clear purpose. This gives the balcony the feeling of an outdoor room rather than a collection of unrelated pots and furniture.

A crispy wave fern in a pot adds texture and visual interest. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

A practical storage solution helped support the new layout. The face of a second-hand barbecue trolley was clad with upcycled floorboards, creating a neat place to store potting mix and gardening supplies — like a tiny garden shed — which blends seamlessly into the design.

A relaxed seating area, showing how greenery can soften the space and create a welcoming place to sit and enjoy the garden. (ABC News: Madelena Rehorek)

By combining some large feature plants, edible garden beds, vertical planting and clearly defined zones, Tilly and Nick's balcony is now somewhere they genuinely want to spend time.

What was once an underused outdoor area is now a place to cook, garden, read, relax and entertain.

Catch up on the Gardening Australia episode "Balconies, courtyards and small gardens" on iview.

title: 'Sell or put up with it': Changed regulations have redrawn housing battle lines
text:
Residents of a leafy Melbourne street are getting a glimpse of what the future could hold for their neighbourhood, and it's a dramatic departure from the low-rise streetscape they know.

In Armadale, in the Liberal-held electorate of Malvern, plans have been lodged with the council for a six-storey development on Mercer Road, about 900 metres away from the train station.

The developer intends to demolish five single-storey units and build a six-storey block of apartments. If approved, there would be 29 two-three bedroom apartments and two levels of underground parking.

A render of an apartment development that is proposed for Armadale. (Supplied)

Dave Corrigan lives in an apartment across the road and described the plan as outrageous.

"[It's] enough to almost make me consider moving, to be honest," he told 7.30.

"I could probably understand on a main road and High Street … but in the middle of Mercer Road, that's just ridiculous."

Under Labor's new "deemed to comply" planning rules, Mr Corrigan's objections carry limited weight and his right to appeal has been stripped away.

Dave Corrigan opposes the plan and the government regulations. (ABC News)

"Deemed to comply" means that if a development meets a series of standards set out by the government, it can be approved without the usual scope for objections or appeals.

The rules took effect in April, with Labor arguing it would reduce red tape, speed up housing approvals and give developers greater certainty.

With the state election approaching, Labor's high-rise housing plans are becoming a political test: as residents push back against towers in their neighbourhoods and the Coalition pledges to scrap the activity centres and return planning powers to councils.

Labor's plan to build up

Under the Victorian Labor government's activity centres plan, designated areas around major train and tram routes are being opened to more intensive housing development, including buildings of up to 20 storeys or higher in some locations.

Armadale, in the City of Stonnington, is among 60 designated activity centres.

Some residents in Armadale aren't happy about the new six-storey development. (ABC News: Kathleen O'Connor)

Labor says Victoria needs an estimated 2.24 million additional homes by 2051, with at least 70 per cent targeted for established areas.

The federal government has targeted building 1.2 million new homes nationally by 2030.

State Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny says the existing planning system failed to provide enough housing in areas where people want to live.

"We've acted to say that the status quo is no longer an option," Ms Kilkenny told 7.30.

"We cannot continue to have a planning system that continues to lock out Victorians from living in places where they want to live."

The policy has drawn fierce opposition from residents and councils who argue the changes will alter the character of established suburbs, while limiting their ability to influence what gets built.

Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr said residents often assumed taller buildings would be concentrated around railway stations and major roads, but that was no longer the case and councils have been stripped of meaningful influence over decisions that would fundamentally change their communities.

"Council's involvement is minimal because if they tick the government's planning boxes now, residents have no right to object, they have no appeal rights and council has very limited ability to make changes to those proposed developments," Mayor Sehr said.

Box Hill: The future of high-rise Melbourne?

East of Melbourne's CBD, Box Hill offers an example of what a shift towards high-density housing could look like.

Danny Todica lives in a 30-storey apartment block, in Box Hill. (ABC News)

Danny Todica lives there with his partner in a two-bedroom apartment in a 30-storey tower.

The 52-year-old said the convenience of apartment living is hard to beat.

"We have the highway just there, we have the shopping centre just around the corner here, so it's in walking distance of everything and the tram stop is just out there," Mr Todica said.

" People still need to live somewhere. What you can do is give people opportunity to live in a great spot. "

Phil Ward has lived in Box Hill for 47 years. He once campaigned against high-rise development but in 2016 bought an apartment in the 36-storey Sky One tower he had opposed.

"If you can't beat them, join them," he said.

Phil Ward has lived in Box Hill for 47 years. (ABC News)

Mr Ward enjoys the convenience of being able to reach shops and public transport within minutes, but he said the transformation had come at a cost.

He said traffic congestion was now a major concern, while green space was increasingly under pressure from development.

"It only takes a little glitch and all of a sudden gridlock," Mr Ward said.

Box Hill is a major transport hub with the busy Whitehorse Road cutting through the centre, linking to the Maroondah Highway and the eastern suburbs.

But its congestion problem extends beyond one busy road. A 2025 government report found several major roads in the suburb were nearing capacity.

Now, construction work for Labor's multi-billion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop is bringing lane closures and pedestrian detours to the busy centre.

Box Hill illustrates the challenge facing governments trying to accommodate a growing population and how to provide more homes while maintaining liveability and updating infrastructure.

Ms Kilkenny said new developments in activity centres would attract infrastructure contributions to help fund parks, schools, road upgrades and community facilities as populations grow.

Who gets the final say?

For residents and councils opposed to Labor's plan, the issue is not simply how tall new buildings should be. It is whether local communities still have a meaningful say in what happens around them.

Ms Kilkenny rejected the suggestion that councils had lost their influence.

Victorian Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny rejects the claim that council's have lost their influence. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"Our deemed to comply planning applications will mean that if the development meets those various standards, there is no capacity to object to that and they will be approved," she said.

Mayor Sehr said that left residents with little choice when a proposal met the new state rules.

"They either sell or just put up with it," she said.

Dr Stephen Glackin, Senior Research Fellow in urban planning at Swinburne University of Technology said the Labor government is trying to use the existing infrastructure.

"The more we expand, it's just more expensive and it's leaving the people who are on the fringes of the city open to travel poverty. They might have an affordable house, but getting into the jobs is going to be really difficult," he said.

"If there's already train lines there, why not build around them? If there's already plumbing and electricity there, build around them. Sure you're going to have to upgrade some stuff, but it's largely there already."

The Coalition has promised to scrap Labor's activity centres policy if elected, return third-party appeal rights to residents and give councils a greater role in planning their communities.

There are a number of apartment towers in Box Hill. (ABC News)

"We believe that local communities should have a say in how their community grows," Opposition Leader Jess Wilson told 7.30.

Ms Wilson said a Coalition government would shift the focus of high-rise development to Melbourne's CBD and inner city, rather than impose Labor's density targets on established suburban neighbourhoods.

"We all know the need to build more homes right across this state, but what we want to do is make sure that we actually deliver more homes and more choice," she said.

She then attacked Labor's record on regional development.

"We want to see a mix of homes right across this state," Ms Wilson said.

"We''ve seen in Geelong, for example, precincts that have been designated for new homes sit there idle for years under this Labor government because they have not acted."

title: Man United legend lashes current players for behaving 'like babies'
text:
Manchester United's all-time leading scorer Wayne Rooney has labelled the club's current players selfish, lashing them for behaving "like babies" after captain Bruno Fernandes questioned the coaching staff's tactics following their Champions League thrashing by Como.

Fernandes said United failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a "mood of defeat" after conceding in the second minute, as Thursday morning's 4-1 loss intensified scrutiny of manager Michael Carrick.

United's collapse at Como left them staring at another damaging result, with only a stoppage-time goal from Joshua Zirkzee reducing the margin of defeat.

Man United captain branded 'disgrace' for comments following latest loss Bruno Fernandes takes aim at Michael Carrick as Manchester United's horrible start to the season goes from bad to worse in the Champions League.

The criticism follows signs of growing frustration within the squad. Earlier this month, defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club's hierarchy after a 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid, saying he expected greater investment to help the team compete at the highest level.

"When Martinez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart," Rooney told the United Stand podcast on Thursday.

"That was the start. We've seen it now with Bruno, and you're going to see it with more players because they don't want to take responsibility.

"You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said, but you have to take responsibility on the pitch. You have to take responsibility as a group of players.

Wayne Rooney (right) was a long-time teammate of current United boss Michael Carrick (left). (Getty Images)

"These players, they're selfish. They don't care about their teammates, don't care about the manager, the staff or the fans, they care about themselves.

"If they're not getting what's right for them, they're like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves."

Carrick, a former United midfielder who played alongside Rooney at Old Trafford, was appointed on an interim basis following Ruben Amorim's dismissal in January before earning a contract through 2028 after overseeing a dramatic improvement in results.

Carrick is under growing pressure with United winless in seven matches across all competitions. They are 20th in the Champions League standings and 13th in the Premier League.

Reuters

title: Mayor told staff member to 'lose some weight', misconduct probe finds
text:
A regional South Australian mayor said a staff member "needs to go back to netball and lose some weight", an investigation into alleged breaches of behavioural standards has found.

District Council of Robe Mayor Lisa Ruffell has led the council, located about 350 kilometres south-east of Adelaide on the state's Limestone Coast, since 2023.

In June, the council ordered an independent investigation into allegations she had undermined the professional reputation of council employees, contributed to distress, created governance instability and contributed to psychosocial risks for staff.

On Wednesday, the council published an investigation summary report as part of papers for a special meeting scheduled for Monday.

The Kelledy Jones Lawyers investigation outlined its findings across seven pages, including that Ms Ruffell said a staff member "needs to go back to netball and lose some weight" while at a community photo shoot for council grant recipients.

It identified multiple instances of Ms Ruffell allegedly criticising council staff in public settings, including telling one employee an asset could be fixed "if it wasn't for your big fat salary" while at a meeting with state government representatives unrelated to that asset.

District Council of Robe CEO Nat Traeger with Lisa Ruffell. (Supplied: District Council of Robe)

Ms Ruffell was also found to have discussed council business and employee matters with community members, including describing employees as "lazy" and saying "they don't do anything".

This was in addition to multiple instances where the investigation described Ms Ruffell as "dismissive" in meetings and would "roll her eyes" while staff spoke.

Investigators also reviewed "rude, undermining and disrespectful" emails sent by Ms Ruffell to employees.

The investigation stated Ms Ruffell was first made aware of the allegations in February, before she responded a month later.

The matter was referred to the local government Behavioural Standards Board, which recommended the council contract independent lawyers to conduct the investigation.

Mayor denies findings

The investigation will be tabled to a council meeting on Monday night, where Ms Ruffell will be absent from discussion due to conflict of interest protocols.

There, elected members will vote on whether to censure Ms Ruffell.

The investigation noted the mayor disputed the findings in full and stated she submitted "the report does not adequately identify the evidence relied on" and "that adverse witness material was not provided to her in full".

Ms Ruffell told the ABC she would wait until Monday's meeting to comment further, but she "strongly" disputed the investigation's findings and had concerns about its process.

"I am also disappointed that the publicly available meeting papers contain only the investigator's summary, rather than the full report," she said.

" I believe the community deserves a fuller understanding of the material being relied upon. "

The investigation noted a failure to come to a private resolution over the complaints necessitated them being discussed at a public council meeting.

Ms Ruffell said she had sought informal resolution and mediation "from the outset" and the decision to pursue a formal investigation "was not mine".

Three months after Consumer Protection issued a warning over a Perth house relocation company alleged to have left around 40 people $6 million out of pocket collectively, questions are now being raised about why it is still operating. Perth House Relocators, also known as JT Projects and JST Projects Australasia, is run by 35-year-old James Sinclair Thomson. James Sinclair Thomson. Consumer Protection WA He buys old homes and removes them, selling them on, charging clients for transportation, as well as development plans, council approvals, renovations, additions, site earthworks and plumbing installation. But over the past 12 months, Thomson has been accused by a growing list of people of being a scammer. They say he has not honoured contracts, takes deposits without supplying them with a house, owes contractors pay for work, and hotels for accommodation and food.

Sinclair told this masthead in June that he strenuously denied the allegations. Weeks later Consumer Protection released a warning against engaging with Thomson after nine separate complaints were made. Now it’s alleged those complaints have risen, while Thomson continues operating. On Thursday, WA Nationals leader Shane Love took growing concerns to parliament, asking Commerce Minister Tony Buti what action had been taken to stop Thomson from continuing to operate. “My office has received significant additional complaints regarding Mr Thomson, which far exceeded the volume reported by Consumer Protection,” he said.

Love cited families who were left out of pocket by hundreds of thousands of dollars after paying Thomson for a house they either never received, or was so unfinished they couldn’t live in it. Leanne Green “I ask the minister, has Consumer Protection received any further complaints about work solicited, contracted, or paid for after its July warning?” Love said. “Has it established whether Mr Thomson continued advertising or accepting the inquiries under his various business names, and what further enforcement action has been taken against Mr Thomson?”

Consumers should not be left carrying the risk simply because a building business operates under a different model.” Buti said that since the Consumer Protection warning about Thomson, three more complaints have been made, before adding that “the penalty for an offence of this nature under the Australian Consumer Law is up to $100 million for a company, or two-and-a-half million dollars for an individual.” “I’ve asked the Building Commissioner to provide me with advice on how the regulatory framework should respond to the growing use of modern methods of construction, including modular and prefabricated housing, to strengthen protection for Western Australian consumers,” he said.

Flagship Minerals has just honed a sharper edge on its option to acquire the high-grade Rosario copper-silver project in Chile by renegotiating its deal with vendor Sociedad Minera Rajo SpA. The revised agreement extends the purchase option to October 2028 and halves the final exercise payment to just US$1 million (A$1.42M), giving it a cheaper path to securing 100 per cent ownership of the project.

The company has already made a US$100,000 payment for the current year and has another US$100,000 (A$142,450) payment due later this month, before making the final exercise payment in 2028.

Flagship Minerals Rosario copper project, where old workings exhibit characteristic blue-green copper oxide staining on joint planes.

Flagship says it retains the flexibility to make the payments in either cash or shares and can exercise the final option early, thereby waiving any outstanding annual payments. The deal also includes a one per cent net smelter royalty, which the company can buy back at an agreed price.

The Rosario project is the cornerstone of Flagship’s Chilean copper strategy. It sits at an altitude of 2500 metres in the commune of Diego de Almagro, within the Chañaral Province of the Atacama region, 125 kilometres east of the coastal port city of Chañaral. Most notably, it sits in a highly active mining district, 160km north of the major mining city of Copiapó and just 10km north of state-owned mining giant Codelco’s massive 2.2-billion-tonne El Salvador copper mine, which contains 9Mt of the red metal.

title: Why millions of overseas basketball fans are following Sydney's newest star
text:
In Brief Chinese Olympian Yang Shuyu has brought millions of followers' attention to the WNBL.

Four Chinese national team players and a new broadcast deal are growing the league's reach in China.

A Chinese Olympian with more than five million followers has made a winning start to life in Australia, helping the Sydney Flames to a dominant victory while drawing fresh attention to the Women's National Basketball League (WNBL) from fans across China.

Yang Shuyu scored 20 points in her first home game for the Flames on Saturday, helping guide the club to a 95-68 win over the Adelaide Lightning.

But the 24-year-old's arrival is about more than one player.

Yang — who has 5.3 million followers on Douyin, the Chinese equivalent of TikTok — is one of four Chinese national team stars in the league this season, as the WNBL looks to strengthen its presence in China and reach new audiences across Asia.

From China to Sydney

Yang joined the Flames earlier this year after building an impressive career in China.

The guard represented China at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, helping the country's 3x3 team win bronze. She was also part of the squad that won the 2023 Women's Asia Cup.

Fans cheer during the Sydney Flames' season opener, which drew a record opening-round crowd for the club. Source: Supplied

Speaking to SBS Mandarin, Yang said the move to Australia was driven by a desire to experience a different style of basketball.

"I've always wanted to play in different countries and experience different systems and styles of basketball," she said.

"I think that can help me improve."

Yang said she was already enjoying life in Sydney, both on and off the court.

"It feels great, and the weather is really nice. Everyone has been very kind to me, and I'm really looking forward to joining this big family."

'Already a star'

The excitement surrounding Yang's arrival was evident before she even stepped onto the court.

The Flames' season opener drew the largest opening-round crowd in club history, with many supporters telling SBS Mandarin they had come specifically to watch the Chinese star play.

"We're here to watch the Sydney Flames and support Yang Shuyu," one fan said.

"We hope she plays well and we hope she enjoys living in Sydney."

Yang Shuyu's growing fanbase was on display at the Flames' season opener. Source: Supplied

Another supporter said Yang had already become one of China's most recognisable basketballers.

"She's already a star in our national team," they said.

"We hope she can make her mark in an overseas league and show what she can do."

The attention Yang generated was matched by her performance.

She finished with 20 points, three rebounds and a steal, tying with teammate Jaz Shelley as the game's leading scorer in the Flames' 27-point win.

Flames coach Renae Garlepp said Yang had already made an impression despite only recently joining the squad.

"I think she played really well, and I'm happy for her," Garlepp said.

"What's great about her goes beyond the way she plays basketball. She's fitted into the team so easily.

"She's a lovely person and genuinely wants to be a good teammate. We're very lucky to have her."

Australian league sees rise in new Chinese fans

Yang's arrival also reflects a broader push by the WNBL to strengthen its connection with Chinese basketball fans.

She's one of four Chinese national team players competing in the league this season, alongside Southside Melbourne Flyers' Wang Siyu and Geelong Venom pair Zhang Wanglai and Han Xu.

WNBL chief operations officer Justin Nelson said the league had already seen growing interest from new audiences.

"Excitingly, we saw a huge rise in new fans, especially coming out to support the four Chinese national players and the high number of Opals playing this season," he said.

The Flames' season opener attracted a record opening-round crowd as the WNBL reported rising attendance and engagement. Source: Supplied

According to the league, opening-round attendance was up 40 per cent on last season, while social media engagement also reached record levels.

The growing interest comes as the WNBL expands its footprint in China. Last week, the league announced a broadcast partnership with Chinese media company YIDA that will make every game of the 2026-27 season available across Douyin, RedNote, Kuaishou and WeChat.

Nelson said the league hoped basketball could help build stronger connections between Australia and China.

"We hope basketball can serve as a bridge between the two countries, creating new opportunities for sporting exchange and new points of connection between Chinese and Australian cultures," he said.

Yang said she hopes to play a role in that exchange during her time in Australia.

"I'm really looking forward to meeting local fans and taking part in community events," she said.

"I also hope to bring some Chinese basketball culture here and build connections through sport."

title: A $3 billion downgrade could send a ripple through a surging Australian industry
text:
When energy provider Jemena announced on Wednesday that it had paused the installation of new 22-metre-tall concrete power poles needed for a nearby data centre, it triggered a chain reaction.

One of the country's biggest data centre operators, NEXTDC — which was forced to delay a planned expansion of its M3 data centre in West Footscray, Melbourne — quickly saw its market valuation drop by around $3 billion.

The plunge was equivalent to about 42 per cent of the company's value, which could send fears through a surging sector still reeling from the failed float of one of its other biggest players.

Luke Laretive, CEO of Seneca Financial Solutions, said fear of "a significant downgrade" to NEXTDC's future earnings and a "contagion-type vibe" had spooked the share market.

"Are [data centre operators] going to be in a position now where ... despite having insatiable demand, they're unable to actually build these facilities in locations that have access to power, water, a community that's happy to have them nearby and are still close enough to the businesses and the people that want to use them?" the investment adviser told SBS' On The Money.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Some of the community around NEXTDC's West Footscray facility seemingly aren't happy to have it nearby. Local residents have previously expressed fears about the amount of diesel stored on the site and raised concerns about noise pollution.

The installation of the power poles required to meet the facility's significant electricity needs has also sparked community anger, with some residents of a nearby suburb using their cars and bins to block equipment deployed for the electricity network upgrade in September.

"Has NEXTDC lost its social licence to operate here, or have data centre providers more generally lost their social licence to operate?" Laretive asked.

Data centres and social licence

Less than two weeks earlier, data centre operator Firmus Technologies withdrew its application for public listing on the Australian Stock Exchange — a move that had been touted as the biggest since Telstra's 1997 float.

Firmus Technologies operates a data centre in Melbourne and is currently building another in Tasmania, with plans for at least two more — despite facing some community backlash.

A month before cancelling its public listing, Firmus announced several-year sponsorship deals with the Tasmania Devils AFL teams, Cricket Tasmania, and Tasmania JackJumpers and Jewels basketball teams, raising concerns of 'sportswashing'.

Olivia Shen, director of strategic technologies at the University of Sydney's United States Studies Centre (USSC), thinks the social licence for data centres could be in the process of being lost across Australia.

"The build-out has been incredibly fast and incredibly rapid," she said.

"And I think at the local level, communities are just feeling quite blindsided by all this development, and especially where it's happening on very large scale in areas where they're not used to this kind of development."

This sentiment conflicts with government messaging that, according to Shen, is more focused on a "narrative that these data centres are incredibly important public facilities for AI development".

That narrative may not be cutting through, with the USSC's 2025 annual poll finding that 67 per cent of Australians "want to prioritise the regulation of AI even at the cost of innovation".

"These Australians are basically saying that even if it slows innovation, we want to progress at a bit of a slower pace rather than having these technologies being shoved down our throats and being told that they're actually good for us," she said.

Some residents living near Next DC's M3 data centre in Melbourne's West Footscray have protested against the development. Source: AAP / Christopher Hopkins

However, Shen said people should be careful in making broad generalisations about the entire industry.

"Not all data centres are the same, not all of the technologies they use are the same from one operator to another, and the impact on the community really, really depends on the local conditions of that community," she said.

A data centre reliant on a polluting energy plant planning to build next to rural farmland used for cattle production will have a different impact to one hoping to build in a quiet suburb in the city.

Laretive, meanwhile, suggested data centre operators "learn from the likes of the BHP's and the Rio [Tinto]'s of the world" for community engagement.

"They are a real participant in the community, and they're not just there kind of soaking up resources," he said, referencing jobs created by mining companies.

Fears history is repeating itself

The Western Downs Digital Park is a $32 billion proposed data centre in Queensland. AI giant Anthropic signed a lease for the first of four planned buildings, but the site has not yet received approval.

Luke Munn, an Australian Research Council future fellow with the University of Queensland, and Joanna Horton, a postdoctoral research fellow, are studying the proposed site.

"I think what we've seen in the last couple of years is a kind of increasing recognition from the public that there's an infrastructure and a material footprint around the AI boom," Munn said.

Horton said the community have been "really pushing back against the proposed development".

The proposed design for the Western Downs Digital Park. Source: Supplied / Urbis

A petition to stop the project already has 23,496 signatures — the most support for any active e-petition on the Queensland parliament website.

"It has been a hotspot for gas extraction, which has been a really big 'boom and bust' industry for the region," she said.

It's left residents concerned about history repeating, with new jobs being created only to disappear before too long. Another concern is natural resource extraction and water use, which critics have said could have a significant impact on the drought-prone region.

Horton said locals are also taking action, with the Environmental Defenders Office, a non-profit community legal centre, reporting a 250 per cent increase in inquiries related to data centres since January of this year.

Protesters gathered outside the Senate inquiry into data centre regulatory frameworks earlier this year. Source: AAP / James Ross

"I think that shows that all over Australia really are seeing data centres as a) something that they're not sure about that they have very real concerns about, and then b) something that they actually want to take action and push back on," she said.

Munn added that some companies now saw potential community opposition as a more important factor than geography or energy supply when choosing potential sites for data centres.

Is the data centre bubble starting to pop?

Shen doesn't think challenges faced by companies like Firmus are necessarily a sign that Australia's data centre boom is over, but she sees it as a warning that not every data centre company will see its investment pay off.

"There are firms jumping on this data centre bandwagon that are probably not going to be the best firms," she said.

"This is complex physical and digital infrastructure, and I don't think every single investor in a data centre is necessarily going to make their money back."

She says it could be a good thing if it encourages "more level-headedness with people investing in the right places".

Laretive said the NEXTDC case likely doesn't say too much about the demand for AI, but he still urges caution for investors.

"We need to be careful about evaluations and the amount of the future that we price into today's numbers and today's market capitalisation."

Meta and its social media platforms Facebook and Instagram are facing a class action lawsuit in Australia over allegations that addictive design features are harming children and teenagers.

The suit filed in the Federal Court on behalf of eight applicants seeks to recover compensation for Facebook and Instagram users who were exposed to harmful content or developed an addiction to social media, law firm Minter Ellison and Litigation Lending said in a statement.

The Federal Court in Sydney issued a suppression order on Monday stopping publication of details of the claim and the identity of the applicants, court documents show.

"We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously," a Meta spokesperson said in a statement.

Litigation Lending Services said it was funding the class action for Australian families who "would have no practical means of pursuing these claims against a global technology giant".

"This proceeding raises important questions about the design and operation of social media platforms and their impact on children and teenagers in Australia," Minter Ellison partner William Nolan said in a statement.

The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and big tech after a world-first ban on social media for children under 16, and newly proposed rules that could let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to US$17.7 billion (roughly $25 billion) in the United States to settle claims that it deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users.

Meta ordered to pay US$25 billion in New Mexico

News of the Australian lawsuit came shortly after a judge in the US state of New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay US$25 billion ($35.2 billion) after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in US President Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from ‌millions of Facebook users without their consent.

New Mexico attorney general Raúl Torrez said it was one of the largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against a company in US history.

"Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.

Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.

In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said.

"At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."

The company had previously said a penalty in the billions of dollars risked violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines.

title: Flights will soon take off from Australia's newest airport. Here's where they're going
text:
In Brief Sydney's second airport opens on Sunday, offering 24-hour flights and new domestic and international routes.

Seven airlines have signed on, taking jetsetters to both domestic and international locations.

Sydney's second airport is about to open, marking the first new international airport built in Australia in more than 50 years.

Western Sydney International Airport, officially named Nancy-Bird Walton Airport, will welcome its first passengers on 25 October.

Located at Luddenham near Badgerys Creek, about 45km from Sydney's CBD, the airport is expected to reshape travel across Greater Sydney, offering an alternative to Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport and providing airlines access to a 24-hour aviation hub.

From flight routes and transport links to where it's located and how it differs from Sydney Airport, here's everything you need to know.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Where can you fly from Western Sydney International Airport?

Western Sydney International Airport will have one significant advantage over Sydney's existing airport: it can operate around the clock.

Unlike Kingsford Smith Airport, which is subject to an overnight curfew between 11pm and 6am, flights at the new airport can arrive and depart 24 hours a day.

That flexibility has helped attract domestic and international carriers, with seven airlines already committing to operate services from the airport.

Here's where they'll fly:

Qantas: Four weekly flights to Melbourne and Brisbane from March 2027.

Jetstar: Four weekly flights to the Gold Coast, three weekly flights to Brisbane, and daily services to Melbourne.

Qatar Airways: Three weekly flights to Doha's Hamad International Airport from 15 December, with additional services planned in coming years.

Air New Zealand: Three weekly flights to Auckland from 26 October.

Singapore Airlines: Daily flights to Singapore from 23 November.

Fiji Airways: Three weekly flights to Nadi.

Vietjet Air: Two weekly flights to Ho Chi Minh City from 10 January 2027, increasing to three in March 2027, plus four weekly flights to Bangkok via Vietjet Thailand.

Emirates has also been cleared to add seven weekly flights from the airport but is yet to announce a schedule.

Airport operators expect additional airlines and destinations to be announced as passenger numbers grow.

How do you get to Western Sydney International Airport?

One of the biggest questions facing travellers is how they will reach Sydney's newest airport.

Unlike Kingsford Smith Airport, which is connected to Sydney's rail network, Western Sydney International Airport will initially rely on road connections and bus services while major transport infrastructure is completed.

A Sydney Metro line linking the airport with St Marys is under construction and expected to open next year.

Until then, passengers can connect to St Marys via a free airport shuttle bus, or travel by express coach, public bus, taxi, rideshare or private vehicle.

If you're driving, the airport is accessible via the new toll-free M12 Motorway and is about an hour from Sydney's CBD, depending on traffic conditions.

An express shuttle service will also connect the airport with Parramatta, Sydney CBD and Sydney Airport.

Current fares are:

Parramatta: $25 one way, $45 return.

Sydney CBD: $55 one way, $80 return.

Sydney Airport: $65 one way, $90 return.

From St Marys, passengers can connect to Sydney's wider rail network, though journeys to some parts of Sydney may take considerably longer than travelling via Kingsford Smith Airport.

State-run bus services will also link the airport with centres including Penrith, Liverpool, Campbelltown, Mount Druitt and Leppington.

For those driving, the airport has about 6,000 parking spaces available on site.

Where is Western Sydney International Airport?

Western Sydney International Airport is located at Luddenham, near Badgerys Creek, in Sydney's west.

The airport is approximately 45km from Sydney's CBD, 20km from Penrith and 15km from Liverpool.

It sits within the broader Western Sydney Aerotropolis precinct and will become Sydney's second major airport when passenger operations begin on Sunday.

Why is Western Sydney International Airport a big deal?

Plans for a second major Sydney airport have been debated for decades as governments looked for ways to meet the city's growing aviation demand.

The airport is expected to become the centrepiece of the Western Sydney Aerotropolis, a major business and infrastructure precinct that planners hope will drive jobs, investment and development across the region.

When it opens, Western Sydney International Airport will be able to handle up to 10 million passengers a year.

That capacity is expected to expand significantly over coming decades, with airport operators forecasting it could eventually handle 82 million passengers annually.

While flight options will initially be limited, airport operators expect additional airlines and destinations to be added as the airport grows.

Will Western Sydney International Airport make airfares cheaper?

Aviation experts have previously told SBS News that the change will fundamentally alter the country's airfare market and could drive prices down for consumers by opening up air travel capacity.

However with rail links that may not be ready until 2028, getting to the airport could theoretically incur a cost that would be similar or more than the savings on a ticket.

title: Haines' staff speak of 'deeply traumatic' experience caring for MP in aftermath of attack

In brief Supporters are rallying around the MP as the wait for further updates on her condition continues.

The man accused of attacking Helen Haines did not apply for bail and will remain behind bars.

The office of Helen Haines, who remains in a critical condition, has said its members are "devastated" by the attack on the independent MP, adding that their proximity to the incident had made the experience "deeply traumatic".

"Our team is devastated by the attack on Helen Haines this week. Helen is adored by her team. She is a remarkable leader, a truly wonderful boss and someone we all care about deeply," Kaz Rourke, Haines' chief of staff, said in a statement released on Thursday afternoon.

"Most of us were in the office when the incident occurred, and some of us were involved in Helen's immediate care, so this has been deeply traumatic for the team.

"We are receiving a great deal of support and my priority right now is making sure Helen's staff are as okay as they can be. I'm so very proud of them and know Helen would be too."

She added that, while Haines' office remained closed to the public, the team was "working in the background and planning towards reopening later next week".

"It is important to us to keep doing our jobs, for Helen and for the people of Indi.

"Most of all, our hearts right now are with Helen, with Phil, their children and their family."

'Helen is alive and she's stable'

Melbourne's Alfred Hospital said on Thursday afternoon that Haines remains in a critical condition and would likely share another update on Friday morning.

Haines' husband Phil confirmed on Wednesday that the MP has had both her legs amputated and is recovering from multiple surgeries.

"But the good news in all this is Helen is alive and she's stable," he told reporters inside the hospital.

"That is the most important thing for our family."

Governor-General Sam Mostyn said she had the "great honour" to spend time with their broader family before the press conference.

"She's lost both her legs in this horrific attack and how any person, let alone a family then starts to process that," Mostyn told ABC News Breakfast.

"We've just got to continue to have them in our thoughts."

Supporters gathered in Wodonga for a vigil for Indi MP Helen Haines. Source: SBS News / Rayane Tamer

Independent MP Dai Le told SBS Vietnamese she had a "wonderful" conversation with Haines in the most recent parliamentary sitting week.

"Helen told me she was looking forward to the end of the year so she could have some rest. That last conversation with her has stayed with me."

The member for Fowler said it's "very difficult and confronting" to hear what has happened to Haines.

"My thoughts are with her, her husband and their family. It’s also an incredibly difficult time for the Nugent family [Brendan Nugent is accused of the attack], who know Helen. It’s hard to comprehend what has happened, and I feel for everyone involved."

Le said she was determined to keep up her community engagements.

"I will not stop attending community events or surround myself with security simply because of what has happened. I’m part of the people."

A sea of orange cockatoos

The update has brought some relief to her supporters across the electorate, including her predecessor Cathy McGowan.

McGowan won the seat of Indi in 2013, serving as the electorate’s first-ever independent MP until she retired in 2019.

She said the shock is still moving through the community.

Supporters filling a book with well wishes for Helen Haines at a vigil in Wodonga. Source: SBS News / Rayane Tamer

"If it can happen to Helen, it can happen to anybody," she told SBS.

"We no longer think, in rural and regional Australia, with our strong communities, that we're immune.

"It was one of us, in our community, by one of us, and saved by us as well."

Supporters in Wodonga gathered for a vigil on Wednesday evening. Many had brought a cardboard orange cockatoo with them — a symbol throughout Haines' campaign.

Among them was Wodonga resident Susan Gordon-Brown. After moving to the area around a year and a half ago, she says she "can't think of anyone better to help".

"She has this huge constituency, yet she seems to be everywhere," she said.

Wolfgang Huber has been involved in every election Haines and McGowan have been in.

He said both have been really important for the community.

Wolfgang Huber holding his prized orange cockatoo. Source: SBS News / Rayane Tamer

"We are a community that has come from all over the world and we should treasure that," he said.

"If I zip it, I look like any other Australian.

"But as soon as I open my mouth, they'll say 'oh, you're a migrant', and that hurts."

What's next for her alleged attacker?

The man accused of attacking Haines will remain in custody until early next year, while an investigation into the incident continues.

Brendan Nugent has been charged with dangerous driving, intentionally causing serious injury, and a federal offence of causing harm to a public official. Court documents showed additional charges for cultivating and possessing cannabis.

Brendan Nugent faced Wangaratta Magistrates' Court on Wednesday. Source: AAP / Anita Lester

He did not apply for bail and was taken to Melbourne Assessment Prison.

The 43-year-old's next court appearance is scheduled for 4 February 2027, for a committal hearing.

It's alleged he intentionally struck the 65-year-old MP with his Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, northern Victoria, on Monday afternoon.

title: 'Imagine siding with the tech bros': Pocock proposes new levy on big players
text:
In Brief David Pocock has proposed a 5 per cent levy on data centres to generate $500 million by 2030.

Speaking at the National Press Club, the senator suggested independents form a coalition for minority government.

Independent senator David Pocock has called for a levy on data centres he says would raise $500 million by the end of the decade.

He said the government was "starstruck" by foreign AI companies and blind to public sentiment, failing to respond to concerns over the impacts of data centres on communities.

Speaking at the National Press Club, he outlined his vision for a political system beyond the major parties, and suggested independents could form a coalition to govern in minority.

The ACT senator suggested smaller community-interest parties working alongside independents could deliver evidence-based solutions, and shift the national focus to the long term.

Pocock also praised his friend Helen Haines, describing her as "a beacon of integrity".

Haines remains in a critical condition after she was allegedly attacked by a 4WD driver outside her parliamentary office in Wangaratta on Monday.

Data centres

Pocock proposed introducing a 5 per cent levy on data centres from early next year. He said the idea had been costed by the Parliamentary Budget Office and would generate $500 million by 2030.

It would be enough, he said, to cover a year of spending for the Housing Australia Future Fund, contributing to the development of new social and affordable housing.

"We all pay income tax to fund the services we use and rely on, yet these huge multinationals turn over billions and find ways to pay little to no company tax here," he said.

Pointing to a lack of long-term thinking, he said the government is putting data centres and frontier AI development ahead of communities and creatives.

"Imagine siding with the tech bros over almost every Australian author, artist and journo that wants their copyright protected," he said.

Pocock, a member of the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, cited evidence from the Copyright Agency's CEO, who warned Australia risked becoming "a global data laundering hotspot" without stronger copyright protections.

A meeting of the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in October. Source: AAP / Sarah Wilson

Independents working together

Pocock said the current major party system is "letting us down" by prioritising vested interests over community needs.

"Too often people are telling politicians how tough things are, only to get some talking points or a long government shopping list of things they’ve done in response," he said.

"And so people are turning away, turning towards something different or turning off altogether."

Rather than "recycled political candidates, former staffers and others from the political class", he wants more independents to choose to represent their communities, while also contributing to a broader political collective on issues like accountability, gambling and the environment.

The ACT senator said smaller community-focused parties and independents working together would better reflect Australia's regional and generational diversity than the traditional two-party system.

"Australians want a politics where their local representative actually reflects their community’s view — not the position of a party or other vested interest," he said.

He said his model prioritised community needs, the opinions of experts and solutions-oriented thinking.

"We want people who have courage and a commitment to the long-term solutions needed to solve them. People like Dr Helen Haines," he said.

Pocock described Haines as "the MP we all wish we had", emphasising her dedication to democracy, transparency, accountability, care and kindness.

title: Elon Musk has hinted at a SpaceX-Tesla mega merger. Could it really happen?
text:
In brief Special committees have been set up to discuss a union between SpaceX and Tesla.

The possible merger news has sent shares of SpaceX surging.

Elon Musk said he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public on Wednesday (AEDT), driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms.

Asked on a call with analysts about a possible merger, Musk said he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield", but that a combination would be "a good idea".

Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly 5 per cent in after-hours trading following the comments.

Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to study the idea at the request of shareholders.

He added that he could not take part in the talks because of a conflict of interest.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The committees have not agreed on any deal terms, and Musk said there is no guarantee they will, cautioning that treating a merger as certain would be overstating it.

Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those cast in a vote, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle".

READ MORE Musk becomes first trillionaire in history as SpaceX shares soar

Musk has in the past tantalised shareholders with the idea of combining SpaceX and Tesla, citing growing overlap between them. Speculation about the space company buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays bank suggesting last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla's annual meeting in December.

What could a SpaceX-Tesla merger look like?

While Tesla and SpaceX were once seen as largely separate businesses, the lines between them have blurred as Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing, satellite communications, and computing infrastructure, including data centres on Earth and potentially in orbit.

A merger would create a single integrated company at the centre of Musk's long-term vision.

"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab [a planned huge semiconductor fabrication plant] obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation [data centres in space], connectivity," Musk said on Wednesday.

Bringing the companies together could also simplify decision-making. Many of Musk's projects already cut across multiple companies, requiring approvals from separate boards and shareholders. A combined company would give management more freedom to deploy capital, engineering talent and infrastructure where it sees the greatest opportunity.

Musk has long argued that he needs greater influence over Tesla to pursue its AI and robotics strategy. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and holds voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate his influence.

What does it mean for investors?

Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX's rapidly growing Starlink broadband operation, launch services business and future space ventures. SpaceX investors would gain ownership of Tesla's vehicle, energy storage, autonomous driving and robotics businesses.

A merged company could also become one of the world's most valuable corporations, with a market value of about US$3.5 trillion ($4.98 trillion).

Supporters would likely argue that the combined company could allocate capital more efficiently across businesses that are increasingly interdependent.

Critics, however, argue that investors would be assuming exposure to a much broader range of technical, regulatory and execution risks, some of which have little connection to one another.

Where could SpaceX and Tesla work together?

Starlink satellites could provide communications links for Tesla's robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of Optimus humanoid robots. Tesla's battery and energy-storage products could help support SpaceX's growing power needs, including future data-centre projects.

Musk has already announced one major Tesla-SpaceX collaboration, Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project aimed at producing the advanced chips needed for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and Optimus robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-centre ambitions. Musk hopes it can start volume production by late 2028.

Tesla's expertise in large-scale factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialise Starship rocket production, while SpaceX technologies have already appeared in Tesla products, most notably the planned use of rocket-derived components in the next-generation Roadster vehicle.

A merged company could also coordinate efforts to secure strategic supply chains, leveraging Tesla's scale in batteries, semiconductors and manufacturing equipment alongside SpaceX's demand for specialised metals, electronics, propulsion components and satellite hardware.

What are the risks?

The biggest challenges may be geopolitics and regulation.

SpaceX is a major contractor for the US military, intelligence agencies and NASA. Tesla, meanwhile, remains deeply tied to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in vehicle production and sales. That combination could invite heightened scrutiny from US regulators and national-security officials as well as from Beijing.

READ MORE Ukraine depends on this battlefield advantage. Others call the shots

The merger would also face shareholder and governance hurdles. Investors would need to be persuaded that combining two already complex businesses creates more value than keeping them separate. Questions about conflicts of interest, voting control and capital allocation would inevitably follow.

Then there is execution risk. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centres, mobile communications and space infrastructure are all expensive, technically challenging bets. Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not reduce those risks. It would simply place them under one roof.

Twenty-seven years after his old man helped Australia win its last Rugby World Cup, rising Waratahs halfback Teddy Wilson has been named in his first Wallabies squad and will tour the UK next month. Wilson, the son of former Wallabies flanker David Wilson, was included in a 33-man squad named by coach Les Kiss ahead of the four-Test tour. In the second instalment of the new Nations Championship tournament, the Wallabies take on England, Scotland and Wales, and will then play in a final against a yet-to-be-determined Six Nations opponent at Twickenham on the final weekend of November. Teddy Wilson on his way to the try line for the Waratahs against the Crusaders. Getty Images In a squad largely devoid of surprises, Wilson and new Queensland prop Tom Lambert were the only two uncapped players named by coach Les Kiss in an otherwise settled group. Lambert’s inclusion came at the expense of Reds prop Aidan Ross, who has been left out just a few days after starting at loosehead prop in the Wallabies’ loss to the All Blacks at the weekend.

Lambert is currently on tour with Australia A and will play against a USA XV in Nashville on Sunday morning. He and lock Miles Amatosero will both join the Wallabies in London. The main inclusions for Kiss come in the form of much-needed cavalry who missed one or both of the Wallabies’ recent defeats to New Zealand, via injury, suspension or overseas club duty. Star five-eighth Carter Gordon has been named after overcoming a broken leg, suffered in Argentina, and he’ll join a No.10 stable including Declan Meredith and Ben Donaldson, who is fit again after missing the Sydney Bledisloe with a groin injury. Key midfielders Len Ikitau (concussion) and Hunter Paisami (suspension) have both been named, and after missing the Bledisloe series because October was not an international release window, overseas-based stars Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper have returned to the squad for November, which is covered by Regulation 9.

Nick Champion De Crespigny and Jock Campbell were also left out. Elsewhere, Tate McDermott was named in the Wallabies squad as one of the halfbacks, but may return to Australia given his partner is due to give birth in November. Kalani Thomas, who debuted for the Wallabies last weekend in Sydney and will also play for the Australia A side in the USA, is on standby. The Wallabies, who take on England in their opening match on November 9, depart for London next Saturday. “There’s a real buzz among the squad as we prepare for what will be four incredibly demanding matches against high-quality opposition as part of the November Nations Championship Tests,” Kiss said in a statement.

text:
