Flagship Minerals has just honed a sharper edge on its option to acquire the high-grade Rosario copper-silver project in Chile by renegotiating its deal with vendor Sociedad Minera Rajo SpA. The revised agreement extends the purchase option to October 2028 and halves the final exercise payment to just US$1 million (A$1.42M), giving it a cheaper path to securing 100 per cent ownership of the project.

The company has already made a US$100,000 payment for the current year and has another US$100,000 (A$142,450) payment due later this month, before making the final exercise payment in 2028.

Flagship Minerals Rosario copper project, where old workings exhibit characteristic blue-green copper oxide staining on joint planes.

Flagship says it retains the flexibility to make the payments in either cash or shares and can exercise the final option early, thereby waiving any outstanding annual payments. The deal also includes a one per cent net smelter royalty, which the company can buy back at an agreed price.

The Rosario project is the cornerstone of Flagship’s Chilean copper strategy. It sits at an altitude of 2500 metres in the commune of Diego de Almagro, within the Chañaral Province of the Atacama region, 125 kilometres east of the coastal port city of Chañaral. Most notably, it sits in a highly active mining district, 160km north of the major mining city of Copiapó and just 10km north of state-owned mining giant Codelco’s massive 2.2-billion-tonne El Salvador copper mine, which contains 9Mt of the red metal.

The federal government has made a formal offer to the European Space Agency to send Australian of the Year Katherine Bennell-Pegg to space. The 2028 mission to the International Space Station would mark the first time an astronaut flies to space under the Australian flag. Australian of the Year, astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg. Alex Ellinghausen The ESA offered to fly Bennell-Pegg, a qualified astronaut and director of space technology at Australian Space Agency, earlier this year. The ESA offer would have cost Australia more than $100 million, Science Minister Tim Ayres has said. The government has not said how much its counteroffer to the ESA was worth.

Advertisement

“The government has long held an ambition to see an Australian astronaut go to space wearing an Australian flag on their space suit,” Ayres said on Friday morning. The government has made a counter-offer to the ESA on taking Katherine Bennell-Pegg to space in 2028. European Space Agency “The government has been engaging extensively with the private sector, philanthropists, and other levels of government to raise funding to support a space flight – which is a significant cost. We are grateful to the philanthropists who have committed over $6 million in cash, plus in-kind support, and some indicative support from some state governments. “We are grateful for the invitation for Katherine Bennell-Pegg to participate in a future mission to the International Space Station and have written to the European Space Agency with an offer that manages the competing pressures on the budget.” The ESA is expected to make a decision on whether to accept the government’s counter-offer later this year.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Space As space race takes off, Australia has lost our best eyes to the universe Following the offer from ESA in May, a fundraising campaign dubbed #flykatherine launched with the aim of garnering industry and philanthropic support for the mission. Entrepreneurs Jim Whalley and Dick Smith, and companies BHP and Novas Systems, have all committed $1 million to the effort. The federal government asked state governments for funding but only South Australia has committed support. Supporters have argued the mission would generate unprecedented momentum for Australia’s space industry and boost careers in STEM. “This rare opportunity to fly Australia’s astronaut with the European Space Agency is an investment in Australian jobs, research and our next generation of scientists and engineers,” chair of the Space Industry of Association of Australia Darin Lovett said.

Advertisement

“For around $100 million, less than the price of a single coffee for every Australian adult, this is not a ticket to space. It is a down payment on Australia’s future in one of the defining industries of this century.” Some within the space industry have been critical of the idea, given the pricetag of the single spaceflight would well exceed the entire annual budget for the Australian Space Agency. Taxpayers covered Bennell-Pegg’s $466,000 astronaut training with the ESA in 2024. A number of Australians have gone to space, including Dr Andy Thomas and Paul Scully, who flew with NASA under the US flag. Bennell-Pegg would be the first to do so under the Australian flag. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
